Done. src/ccreport/ccu.py replaces bin/ccu.zsh, which is deleted.

Remove the macsetup legacy path auto-migration
description:
The cache, snapshot dir and config were relocated off their macsetup-era paths when this tooling left the macsetup repo. `cache_db.get_connection()` still stats the old cache dir on every open that finds no DB and calls `relocate_legacy_paths()`, and `ccreport migrate` exposes the same move on demand. One month after the move (created 2026-08-10) every machine has run it, so the code is dead weight carrying a legacy path constant, a CLI command and a test module.

Touchpoints:
- src/ccreport/cache_db.py:38-42 — the `_LEGACY_CACHE_DIR` / `_LEGACY_SNAPSHOT_DIR` constants and their comment
- src/ccreport/cache_db.py:465 `_move()` and :482 `relocate_legacy_paths()`
- src/ccreport/cache_db.py:521-523 — the auto-call in `get_connection()`
- src/ccreport/project_identity.py:32-33 — `LEGACY_CONFIG_PATH`
- src/ccreport/ccreport.py:1829 `cmd_migrate()` plus its subparser registration
- tests/test_migrate.py and the `LEGACY_CONFIG_PATH` monkeypatch in tests/conftest.py:35
- any mention in README.md / docs/

Before removing: confirm with the user that no machine of theirs still holds ~/.cache/macsetup/claude or ~/.config/macsetup/claude/ccreport.toml — removing the code strands that data rather than losing it, but it then needs a manual `mv`.
acceptance: No reference to macsetup paths remains in src/ or tests/; `ccreport migrate` is gone from the CLI and its help; `just lint-all` and `just test` pass; vulture_whitelist.py has no leftover entry for the removed symbols.

Bash-served full-line statusline cache, no Python on hits
description:
Serve a cache hit entirely from the bash wrapper, so a render costs no Python process at all.

Today every render execs python and goes through src/ccreport/statusline.py, even on the fast path: renders within FAST_TTL_S (15 s) already skip subprocess spawns and db reads by reusing the previous render's fetch results from a per-session temp file, and the wrapper bin/statusline-command_x.sh already skips the uv resolver. Prior measurement on an M-series machine, warm: ~110 ms before those two changes, ~25-30 ms after. What remains is interpreter startup and module import.

Proposal: cache the fully rendered line, with placeholders for the segments that must stay live. bin/statusline-command_x.sh serves that line on a hit and fills the placeholders itself — clock from $EPOCHSECONDS plus printf strftime, ctx% via jq from the stdin JSON. On a miss it falls through to Python as now. Estimated ~10 ms per hit.

Cost, which is why this is priority 3: a second formatting path in bash, and placeholder splicing that has to be kept in sync with the Python renderer whenever a segment's format changes. Only worth doing if ~25-30 ms still bothers us in practice. Requires bash 5 for $EPOCHSECONDS and printf %(fmt)T — /bin/bash is 3.2, so pin the shebang to the Homebrew bash — and jq on PATH.
acceptance:
- A cache hit renders with no python process spawned (verify with a process trace or a counter).
- Clock and ctx% are correct on every hit, not stale.
- Missing bash 5 or jq falls back to the Python renderer instead of erroring.
- Measured hit latency is reported in the issue before it moves to in_review.
- Tests under tests/ cover the placeholder contract between the Python renderer and the wrapper.

description:
docs/calculation-reference.md:55-70 carries a hand-copied price table headed 'Current Prices (as of LAST_CHECKED = 2026-02-22)'. pricing.py:116 reads LAST_CHECKED = 2026-07-24. docs section 5.5 describes the pre-incremental session cache
description:
docs/calculation-reference.md:443-455 says the session cost fingerprint is an md5 over the sorted (path, mtime_ns, size) tuples, and that a session is re-parsed whenever any file's mtime or size changes.

The code does something else. pricing._encode_session_state stores a versioned JSON blob: a version field, a per-file _FileCursor (mtime_ns, size, offset, tail) and dedup-key digests. pricing._decode_session_state:897 names the md5 shape explicitly as 'the pre-incremental md5 fingerprint' - the legacy form it still reads. A file that grew is resumed from its stored offset and tail digest, not re-parsed from the top.

Why it matters: the doc describes full invalidation where the code does incremental resume. A maintainer chasing a wrong session cost looks for the wrong failure mode, and the real one (a cursor that drifted from the file) is not documented at all.
acceptance: Section 5.5 rewritten around _SessionCostState and _SESSION_STATE_VERSION: what the blob holds, that a version mismatch costs one full reparse, that growth is resumed from offset plus the tail digest, and that the md5 form is legacy read-only. No claim that a changed file is re-parsed whole.

Document the contracts of the public surface: raises, exits, return shapes
description:
Six exported functions have behaviour that callers must handle and no docstring stating it. All are test-covered, so the behaviour is contract rather than accident.

1. pricing.compute_costs (pricing.py:1673) - the Cost buckets list documents 11 keys but the function returns 6 more (six_hour_project_cost through all_time_project_cost). It never states that session_window_cost is OMITTED rather than zeroed when no session reset is known - that omission is what statusline._merge_cost_data and usage_api._run_costs_only are built on, and zeroing it instead would carry the previous window's total across a rollover. The side effect (it caches the result via write_cost_summary) is also unstated.
2. ccreport.load_all_records (ccreport.py:802) - raises ValueError when use_rollups is passed together with since, until, project_filter or account_filter (ccreport.py:825-827). Undocumented.
3. cache_db.prefix_range (cache_db.py:1986) - raises ValueError on an empty prefix, with its own test. Undocumented. The reason is that an empty prefix would silently widen the range to the whole table.
4. ccreport.cmd_limits (ccreport.py:2540) - exits 1 when no samples exist and when the filters match nothing.
5. ccreport.cmd_adopt (ccreport.py:1917) - exits 1 when the capture log is empty.
6. cache_db.compute_extra_window_deltas (cache_db.py:1510) - never names the two keys it returns (extra_session_delta, extra_week_delta) or that None means no snapshot predates that window.

Smaller, same class: cache_db.usage_is_fresh, read_usage_cache and read_cost_summary (:1144, :1172, :3044) never say max_age is in seconds; usage_api.fetch_usage_api (:242) leaves its return contract at 'etc.' though the key set is _API_QUOTA_FIELDS and a test asserts the two are equal, and does not say HTTPError/URLError propagate once retries are exhausted.

Note: pyproject.toml disables D101/D102/D103/D107 deliberately so docstrings carry rationale rather than coverage. This issue is not about adding missing docstrings to internal helpers - it is about documented functions whose stated contract is incomplete.

Explain the constants a maintainer would tune wrong
description:
This tree explains nearly every constant. These are the holes, each judged against its own neighbours in the same file.

1. cache_db.py:535 - PRAGMA cache_size = -2000. The comment explains only why the three pragmas sit outside the version gate, never that the negative sign is SQLite's KiB-versus-pages switch. 'Fixing' it to 2000 means 2000 pages, roughly 8 MB, per connection - on a path the status line opens every render.
2. ccreport.py:121 - CACHE_VERSION = 2 has no bump policy, while cache_db.SCHEMA_VERSION ('BUMP THIS on any change to...') and cache_db.CACHE_SCHEMA_SALT ('Bump this when...') both state theirs. It is also non-obviously not redundant with _script_hash(), which already hashes ccreport.py. So a maintainer either never bumps it or deletes it as dead weight.
3. The 10-minute usage TTL is spelled as a bare literal at four sites with nothing saying they must agree: usage_api.CACHE_MAX_AGE = 600, two max_age: int = 600 defaults in cache_db (:1172, :3044), and statusline.USAGE_FETCH_INTERVAL_S = 600. That is a departure from this tree's rule of deriving key lists from one source and guarding drift with a test. Tuning one leaves the TTL check and the countdown the user reads describing different intervals.
4. statusline.py:125 - COST_SUMMARY_MAX_AGE = 900 is described as how long a cached compute_costs result stays usable, but nothing says it is what actually paces the costs-only refresh (via _fetch_usage's cost_summary is None branch), nor that the 300 s gap from USAGE_FETCH_INTERVAL_S is deliberate. Aligning it to 600 changes how often a detached subprocess rescans the whole JSONL corpus.
5. cache_db.py:1203 - _BACKOFF_SCHEDULE = [45, 120, 240] names the unit and the index but gives no ceiling reasoning. Nothing says the last step must stay under the 600 s fetch interval; past that, one transient failure suppresses fetching indefinitely.
6. cache_db.py:43-44 - _SANITY_DROP_THRESHOLD_PCT = 10.0 and _SANITY_MIN_PRIOR_COUNT = 100 have no comment and are stranded under the legacy-paths block, so they read as belonging to it. The 10% is what decides whether real loss of unrebuildable orphan records gets reported.
7. cache_db.py:1503 - the 31-day snapshot prune. The comment restates the line and leaves 31 unexplained; the deltas this table feeds are the 5 h and 7 d windows, so 31 looks arbitrary. It is there because Extra usage is a monthly quota.

This tree explains nearly every constant. These are the holes, each judged against its own neighbours in the same file.

description:
docs/calculation-reference.md:443-455 says the session cost fingerprint is an md5 over the sorted (path, mtime_ns, size) tuples, and that a session is re-parsed whenever any file's mtime or size changes.

The code does something else. pricing._encode_session_state stores a versioned JSON blob: a version field, a per-file _FileCursor (mtime_ns, size, offset, tail) and dedup-key digests. pricing._decode_session_state:897 names the md5 shape explicitly as 'the pre-incremental md5 fingerprint' - the legacy form it still reads. title: Replace rot-prone literal counts and one-machine anecdotes

description:
Six exported functions have behaviour that callers must handle and no docstring stating it. All are test-covered, so the behaviour is contract rather than accident.

1. pricing.compute_costs (pricing.py:1673) - the Cost buckets list documents 11 keys but the function returns 6 more (six_hour_project_cost through all_time_project_cost). The side effect (it caches the result via write_cost_summary) is also unstated.
2. ccreport.load_all_records (ccreport.py:802) - raises ValueError when use_rollups is passed together with since, until, project_filter or account_filter (ccreport.py:825-827). Undocumented.
3. cache_db.prefix_range (cache_db.py:1986) - raises ValueError on an empty prefix, with its own test. Undocumented. The reason is that an empty prefix would silently widen the range to the whole table.
4. ccreport.cmd_limits (ccreport.py:2540) - exits 1 when no samples exist and when the filters match nothing.
5. ccreport.cmd_adopt (ccreport.py:1917) - exits 1 when the capture log is empty.
6. cache_db.compute_extra_window_deltas (cache_db.py:1510) - never names the two keys it returns (extra_session_delta, extra_week_delta) or that None means no snapshot predates that window.

Smaller, same class: cache_db.usage_is_fresh, read_usage_cache and read_cost_summary (:1144, :1172, :3044) never say max_age is in seconds; usage_api.fetch_usage_api (:242) leaves its return contract at 'etc.' though the key set is _API_QUOTA_FIELDS and a test asserts the two are equal, and does not say HTTPError/URLError propagate once retries are exhausted.

acceptance: Each of the six carries the missing clause: compute_costs lists the project buckets, states the session_window_cost omission rule and the write_cost_summary side effect; load_all_records and prefix_range each have a Raises: ValueError line with the reason; cmd_limits and cmd_adopt each state when they exit 1; compute_extra_window_deltas names both keys and what None means. title: Document the contracts of the public surface: raises, exits, return shapes

description:
This tree explains nearly every constant. These are the holes, each judged against its own neighbours in the same file.

1. cache_db.py:535 - PRAGMA cache_size = -2000. The comment explains only why the three pragmas sit outside the version gate, never that the negative sign is SQLite's KiB-versus-pages switch. 'Fixing' it to 2000 means 2000 pages, roughly 8 MB, per connection - on a path the status line opens every render.
2. ccreport.py:121 - CACHE_VERSION = 2 has no bump policy, while cache_db.SCHEMA_VERSION ('BUMP THIS on any change to...') and cache_db.CACHE_SCHEMA_SALT ('Bump this when...') both state theirs. It is also non-obviously not redundant with _script_hash(), which already hashes ccreport.py. So a maintainer either never bumps it or deletes it as dead weight.
3. The 10-minute usage TTL is spelled as a bare literal at four sites with nothing saying they must agree: usage_api.CACHE_MAX_AGE = 600, two max_age: int = 600 defaults in cache_db (:1172, :3044), and statusline.USAGE_FETCH_INTERVAL_S = 600. That is a departure from this tree's rule of deriving key lists from one source and guarding drift with a test. Tuning one leaves the TTL check and the countdown the user reads describing different intervals.
4. statusline.py:125 - COST_SUMMARY_MAX_AGE = 900 is described as how long a cached compute_costs result stays usable, but nothing says it is what actually paces the costs-only refresh (via _fetch_usage's cost_summary is None branch), nor that the 300 s gap from USAGE_FETCH_INTERVAL_S is deliberate. Aligning it to 600 changes how often a detached subprocess rescans the whole JSONL corpus.
5. cache_db.py:1203 - _BACKOFF_SCHEDULE = [45, 120, 240] names the unit and the index but gives no ceiling reasoning. Nothing says the last step must stay under the 600 s fetch interval; past that, one transient failure suppresses fetching indefinitely.
6. cache_db.py:43-44 - _SANITY_DROP_THRESHOLD_PCT = 10.0 and _SANITY_MIN_PRIOR_COUNT = 100 have no comment and are stranded under the legacy-paths block, so they read as belonging to it. The 10% is what decides whether real loss of unrebuildable orphan records gets reported.
7. cache_db.py:1503 - the 31-day snapshot prune. The comment restates the line and leaves 31 unexplained; the deltas this table feeds are the 5 h and 7 d windows, so 31 looks arbitrary. It is there because Extra usage is a monthly quota.
acceptance: Each of the seven carries a comment stating what breaks if the value moves, in this tree's existing style. The TTL item names one authority and says why the other three are spelled out rather than imported. _SANITY_DROP_THRESHOLD_PCT and _SANITY_MIN_PRIOR_COUNT are moved out from under the legacy-paths block. just lint-all and just test pass.

docs section 5.5 describes the pre-incremental session cache
description:
docs/calculation-reference.md:443-455 says the session cost fingerprint is an md5 over the sorted (path, mtime_ns, size) tuples, and that a session is re-parsed whenever any file's mtime or size changes.

The code does something else. pricing._encode_session_state stores a versioned JSON blob: a version field, a per-file _FileCursor (mtime_ns, size, offset, tail) and dedup-key digests. pricing._decode_session_state:897 names the md5 shape explicitly as 'the pre-incremental md5 fingerprint' - the legacy form it still reads. A file that grew is resumed from its stored offset and tail digest, not re-parsed from the top.

Why it matters: the doc describes full invalidation where the code does incremental resume. A maintainer chasing a wrong session cost looks for the wrong failure mode, and the real one (a cursor that drifted from the file) is not documented at all.
acceptance: Section 5.5 rewritten around _SessionCostState and _SESSION_STATE_VERSION: what the blob holds, that a version mismatch costs one full reparse, that growth is resumed from offset plus the tail digest, and that the md5 form is legacy read-only. No claim that a changed file is re-parsed whole.

description:

description:
Six exported functions have behaviour that callers must handle and no docstring stating it. All are test-covered, so the behaviour is contract rather than accident.

1. pricing.compute_costs (pricing.py:1673) - the Cost buckets list documents 11 keys but the function returns 6 more (six_hour_project_cost through all_time_project_cost). 2. ccreport.load_all_records (ccreport.py:802) - raises ValueError when use_rollups is passed together with since, until, project_filter or account_filter (ccreport.py:825-827). Undocumented.
3. cache_db.prefix_range (cache_db.py:1986) - raises ValueError on an empty prefix, with its own test. Undocumented. The reason is that an empty prefix would silently widen the range to the whole table.
4. ccreport.cmd_limits (ccreport.py:2540) - exits 1 when no samples exist and when the filters match nothing.
5. ccreport.cmd_adopt (ccreport.py:1917) - exits 1 when the capture log is empty.

acceptance: Each of the six carries the missing clause: compute_costs lists the project buckets, states the session_window_cost omission rule and the write_cost_summary side effect; load_all_records and prefix_range each have a Raises: ValueError line with the reason; cmd_limits and cmd_adopt each state when they exit 1; compute_extra_window_deltas names both keys and what None means. title: Document the contracts of the public surface: raises, exits, return shapes

description:
This tree explains nearly every constant. These are the holes, each judged against its own neighbours in the same file.

1. cache_db.py:535 - PRAGMA cache_size = -2000. The comment explains only why the three pragmas sit outside the version gate, never that the negative sign is SQLite's KiB-versus-pages switch. 'Fixing' it to 2000 means 2000 pages, roughly 8 MB, per connection - on a path the status line opens every render.
2. ccreport.py:121 - CACHE_VERSION = 2 has no bump policy, while cache_db.SCHEMA_VERSION ('BUMP THIS on any change to...') and cache_db.CACHE_SCHEMA_SALT ('Bump this when...') both state theirs. It is also non-obviously not redundant with _script_hash(), which already hashes ccreport.py. So a maintainer either never bumps it or deletes it as dead weight.
3. The 10-minute usage TTL is spelled as a bare literal at four sites with nothing saying they must agree: usage_api.CACHE_MAX_AGE = 600, two max_age: int = 600 defaults in cache_db (:1172, :3044), and statusline.USAGE_FETCH_INTERVAL_S = 600. That is a departure from this tree's rule of deriving key lists from one source and guarding drift with a test. Tuning one leaves the TTL check and the countdown the user reads describing different intervals.
4. statusline.py:125 - COST_SUMMARY_MAX_AGE = 900 is described as how long a cached compute_costs result stays usable, but nothing says it is what actually paces the costs-only refresh (via _fetch_usage's cost_summary is None branch), nor that the 300 s gap from USAGE_FETCH_INTERVAL_S is deliberate. Aligning it to 600 changes how often a detached subprocess rescans the whole JSONL corpus.
5. cache_db.py:1203 - _BACKOFF_SCHEDULE = [45, 120, 240] names the unit and the index but gives no ceiling reasoning. Nothing says the last step must stay under the 600 s fetch interval; past that, one transient failure suppresses fetching indefinitely.
6. cache_db.py:43-44 - _SANITY_DROP_THRESHOLD_PCT = 10.0 and _SANITY_MIN_PRIOR_COUNT = 100 have no comment and are stranded under the legacy-paths block, so they read as belonging to it. The 10% is what decides whether real loss of unrebuildable orphan records gets reported.
7. cache_db.py:1503 - the 31-day snapshot prune. The comment restates the line and leaves 31 unexplained; the deltas this table feeds are the 5 h and 7 d windows, so 31 looks arbitrary. It is there because Extra usage is a monthly quota.
acceptance: Each of the seven carries a comment stating what breaks if the value moves, in this tree's existing style. The TTL item names one authority and says why the other three are spelled out rather than imported. _SANITY_DROP_THRESHOLD_PCT and _SANITY_MIN_PRIOR_COUNT are moved out from under the legacy-paths block. just lint-all and just test pass.

description:
None of these carries a wrong fact, so none needs deleting - each needs rewording.

1. statusline.py:1 - 'Claude Code status line - Python implementation for performance'. No checkable property; residue from the shell-to-Python rewrite. The real facts (renders on every frame, imports nothing outside the stdlib, defers cache_db into the functions that touch it) are stated further down and in AGENTS.md. Either shorten to the bare title or state the property.
2. bin/statusline-command_x.sh:2 - 'Seam Claude Code settings.json points at'. The tree calls this a wrapper everywhere else: README.md ('Point Claude Code settings.json at the wrapper'), bin/ccreport:2 ('A wrapper rather than a symlink'), AGENTS.md ('bin/ holds the wrappers'). One file renames the thing. Note that ccu.py:9's use of 'seam' is precise - it names the boundary the tests stub - and should stay.
3. exchange.py:3-4 - 'Fetches from the Norges Bank SDMX-JSON API, caches in SQLite, and provides rate lookups with automatic fallback for weekends and holidays'. The third item restates the first two; 'provides rate lookups' dodges a plain verb and 'automatic' adds nothing a caller can act on.
4. justfile:13 - '# run all formatters' above fmt-all: just fmt. There is exactly one, and AGENTS.md explicitly forbids adding a second ('Do not add ruff format to a recipe'). The plural invites the edit the project rules out.
